group.title: Crime and justice
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: The room where a legal trial takes place.
examples: The {courtroom} was silent as the judge spoke.
wrong: A courtroom is a place where people play tennis.

words.meaning: A person who saw a crime or accident happen.
examples: An {eyewitness} saw the driver run the red light.
wrong: The eyewitness was asleep at home and saw nothing.

words.meaning: A person held prisoner by criminals until their demands are met.
examples: The robbers held three bank workers {hostage}.
wrong: The hostage was free to leave the building whenever he liked.

words.meaning: An official decision by a court that someone is guilty.
examples: He has two previous {convictions} for driving offenses.
wrong: His conviction showed that the court believed he was innocent.

words.meaning: A crime or an illegal act.
examples: Driving without a license is a serious {offense}.
wrong: Helping an old lady cross the road is an offense.

words.meaning: A person who has committed a crime.
examples: Young {offenders} are often given community work.
wrong: An offender is a person who has never broken the law.

words.meaning: Money that criminals demand before they will free someone they have taken.
examples: The kidnappers asked for a {ransom} of a million dollars.
wrong: A ransom is a reward the police give to good citizens.

words.meaning: To make a formal statement about what you know in a court.
examples: Two neighbors agreed to {testify} at the trial.
wrong: She testified by staying silent and refusing to speak.

words.meaning: A lawyer who tries to prove in court that someone is guilty.
examples: The {prosecutor} showed the jury the video.
wrong: The prosecutor tried hard to prove that the man was innocent.

words.meaning: The crime of setting fire to property on purpose.
examples: The fire at the warehouse was caused by {arson}.
wrong: The fire was arson, so it started by accident from lightning.

words.meaning: An attack on someone in a public place in order to steal from them.
examples: There has been a rise in {muggings} near the station.
wrong: The mugging was a friendly chat between two strangers in the park.

words.meaning: The crime of tricking people to get money.
examples: He was jailed for credit card {fraud}.
wrong: The fraud was an honest deal that cheated no one.

words.meaning: Money or a gift given to someone to persuade them to act dishonestly.
examples: The official was caught taking a {bribe}.
wrong: A bribe is the honest salary a worker gets each month.

words.meaning: To take goods or people secretly and illegally into or out of a country.
examples: They tried to {smuggle} cigarettes across the border.
wrong: They smuggled the goods by declaring them openly at customs.

words.meaning: To take someone away by force and keep them as a prisoner.
examples: The gang {kidnapped} the businessman and asked for money.
wrong: They kidnapped the child by taking her home safely to her parents.

words.meaning: A violent physical attack on someone.
examples: He was arrested for {assault} after the fight.
wrong: The assault was a friendly hug between two old friends.

words.meaning: Punishment by being killed by the state for a serious crime.
examples: Many countries have ended the {death penalty}.
wrong: The death penalty is a small fine for parking in the wrong place.

words.meaning: A punishment for breaking a law or rule.
examples: The {penalty} for littering is a $200 fine.
wrong: The penalty for breaking the rule was a free holiday.

words.meaning: Unpaid work that an offender is ordered to do instead of going to prison.
examples: He was given 100 hours of {community service}.
wrong: Community service is a well-paid job you apply for.

words.meaning: Permission for a prisoner to leave prison early if they behave well.
examples: She was released on {parole} after three years.
wrong: On parole, he had to stay in his prison cell every day.

words.meaning: A period when an offender lives normally but is watched by an officer instead of going to prison.
examples: He got two years’ {probation} for the theft.
wrong: During probation, nobody checks what he does.

words.meaning: A careful official search for the facts about a crime.
examples: The police have started an {investigation} into the fire.
wrong: The investigation began when the police stopped looking at the case.

words.meaning: The use of force to protect yourself from attack.
examples: He said he hit the man in {self-defense}.
wrong: She acted in self-defense by attacking a stranger who did nothing to her.

words.meaning: Using science to help solve crimes.
examples: {Forensic} experts examined the blood on the shirt.
wrong: The forensic team solved the case without any science at all.

words.meaning: The crime of making a copy of a document or signature to trick people.
examples: The painting turned out to be a {forgery}.
wrong: The forgery was the original letter written by the author herself.

words.meaning: Proof that you were somewhere else when a crime happened.
examples: His {alibi} was that he was at the cinema all evening.
wrong: Her alibi proved she was at the scene of the crime.

words.meaning: Always obeying the law.
examples: Most people are {law-abiding} citizens.
wrong: He’s very law-abiding and steals from shops every week.

words.meaning: To start dealing with a crime or problem much more strictly.
examples: The city is {cracking down on} illegal parking.
wrong: The police cracked down on speeding by ignoring all fast drivers.

words.meaning: Demanding money from someone by threatening to tell their secrets.
examples: He paid the money because of {blackmail}.
wrong: Blackmail is a kind and generous gift to a friend.

words.meaning: To say officially in court that you did the crime.
examples: He {pleaded guilty} to driving too fast.
wrong: She pleaded guilty by telling the court she had done nothing wrong.

words.meaning: Something that makes people decide not to do something.
examples: Cameras act as a {deterrent} to thieves.
wrong: The high fines are a deterrent, so more people break the rule.

words.meaning: To commit a crime again after being punished.
examples: Programs that teach skills help prisoners not to {reoffend}.
wrong: He reoffended by never breaking the law again.

words.meaning: A punishment of spending the rest of your life, or a very long time, in prison.
examples: The murderer received a {life sentence}.
wrong: A life sentence is a two-day stay in prison.

words.meaning: The state of being kept by the police until a trial.
examples: The suspect is being held in {custody}.
wrong: He was in custody, so he was free to go wherever he liked.

words.meaning: An official list of the crimes a person has committed.
examples: Applicants with a {criminal record} cannot work at the school.
wrong: He has a criminal record, so he has never broken the law.

words.meaning: An official paper from a judge that allows the police to do something, such as arrest someone.
examples: The police had a {warrant} to search the house.
wrong: A warrant is a letter that stops the police from doing anything.

words.meaning: A person kept in a prison.
examples: The prison holds about five hundred {inmates}.
wrong: An inmate is a guard who goes home every night.

words.meaning: In prison.
examples: The robber will spend the next ten years {behind bars}.
wrong: He’s behind bars, so he’s free to travel the world.

words.meaning: Crime such as fraud done by people in offices or business jobs.
examples: Stealing from the company accounts is a {white-collar crime}.
wrong: A white-collar crime is a violent street fight between gangs.

words.meaning: Two metal rings joined by a chain, put on a prisoner’s wrists.
examples: The officer put {handcuffs} on the suspect.
wrong: The police put handcuffs on his wrists so he could move his hands freely.
